name: 𐎜𐎂𐎗𐎚
note: Ugaritic, the language of the city of Ugarit (Ras Shamra, on the Syrian coast) in the 14th to 12th centuries BC, in its own cuneiform alphabet of thirty letters, left to right. The alphabet writes consonants only, with three signs for the glottal stop with a, i or u (written ả, ỉ, ủ in the transliteration), so the words are written as the tablets write them, without vowels; words are split by spaces rather than the small word divider, so long lines can wrap. Exported Python prints the usual transliteration (as KTU and the dictionaries write it) instead. About two thousand words survive, from the letters, the administrative tablets and the myths, so many everyday words exist; modern ideas are descriptive coinages on attested roots, used the same way everywhere: ảbn (stone) for block, mknt (what is set up, from kwn) for program, ntb (path) for script, hlk (going) for run, with lk (go!) on the Run button, ṣlm (image, statue) for model, mlảk (messenger) for agent, kly (vessel, implement) for tool, bḥn (test) for review, spr rỉš (first writing) for draft, pr (fruit) for result, mšn (what changes) for variable, lḥ (tablet) for file, ảrn (chest) for folder, mny (counter) for computer, spr ymm (book of days) for calendar, mnt (count, list) for list, dbr (thing, word) for record, šd (field) for a record's field, rṯt (net) for the web, pnt (face, side) for page, ṭbʿ (impression, seal) for token, mpth (opener) for key, mṣb (standing stone) for checkpoint, rgm (word) for message, ỉgrt (letter) for email and brq (lightning) for electricity. Field names, status values, settings, commands and product names stay as they are, in Latin letters, as in the other languages.
